Yoav entra nella sala che è già buio, eppure tutti lo notano: indossa un rekel, la giacca nera che arriva sotto al ginocchio, la camicia bianca, la kippah e ha lunghi peòt che gli coprono le orecchie. Yoav è un ultraortodosso. E nell’auditorium di Tel Aviv colmo di sostenitori di Itamar Ben-Gvir, ministro della Sicurezza nazionale ed esponente di spicco dell’ultradestra al potere in Israele – coloni, nazionalisti, laici ma nessun altro ultrareligioso – spicca come una mosca bianca.

articles.body:
IL PUNTO

Israele al voto per il rinnovo della Knesset: oltre 7,3 milioni di cittadini sono chiamati alle urne, per la prima volta dopo l'attacco del 7 ottobre. Sfida decisiva per il premier Benjamin Netanyahu, che si gioca il futuro politico dopo tre anni di guerra. Seggi aperti fino alle 22 locali: attesi in serata i primi exit poll.

10:27

Netanyahu: 'Ben Gvir farà parte del governo'. Ma lui, 'Bibi andrà con Eisenkot'

''Caro Itamar, quante volte ripeterai questo bluff? Supererai la soglia di sbarramento, farai parte del nostro forte governo di destra guidato da me e continueremo a lavorare insieme per lo Stato di Israele. Un mandato in più o in meno per te non cambierà nulla, ma se Eisenkot otterrà un mandato in più del Likud, il Presidente affiderà a lui il compito di formare un governo e ci ritroveremo con un governo che piangerà per generazioni''. Lo scrive il Likud a nome del premier Netanyahu in una nota, in risposta a quanto affermato dal ministro dell'ultradestra Itamar Ben Gvir, secondo cui Netanyahu ''si è impegnato con l'amministrazione Usa a formare un governo di unità nazionale con Eisenkot e senza di me dopo le elezioni. Se volete un Ben Gvir forte al governo, e non un Ben Gvir debole all'opposizione, ho bisogno del vostro sostegno alle urne'', ha scritto su X Ben Gvir, condividendo un articolo di Israel Hayom che riportano le indiscrezioni secondo cui l'amministrazione Trump starebbe puntando a un governo di unità tra Eisenkot e Netanyahu, che escluda i partiti della destra estremista.

10:27

Affluenza ai seggi del 16,68% alle ore 10 (le 9 in Italia)

La Commissione elettorale centrale israeliana comunica che alle ore 10,00 (le 9 in Italia) l'affluenza alle urne a livello nazionale si attesta al 16,68%, pari a 1.200.000 votanti. Si tratta di un aumento dello 0,78% rispetto alle elezioni del 2022. E' il dato più alto dal 1981. I seggi elettorali aperti sono 12.018 per circa 7,3 milioni di elettori aventi diritto.

10:00

Eisenkot in visita al kibbutz Nir Oz prima di votare

Prima di votare, il presidente di Yashar e principale avversario di Benjamin Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot, ha visitato insieme all'ex ostaggio Gadi Mozes il kibbutz Nir Oz, una delle comunità più colpite dall'attacco del 7 ottobre. "Sono orgoglioso e commosso di iniziare questa giornata con Gadi Mozes, simbolo dello spirito e della forza israeliana, dell'impegno reciproco degli israeliani e del loro impegno verso lo Stato", ha dichiarato Eisenkot. "Mi impegno a fare tutto il possibile per garantire che siamo degni del prezzo che avete pagato, del prezzo pagato dal kibbutz e del prezzo che abbiamo pagato tutti noi, e per portare guarigione e riparazione a tutti i cittadini di Israele", ha detto.

09:25

In Israele familiari degli ostaggi in piazza, 'votate per il cambiamento'

Il presidente israeliano Isaac Herzog è stato tra i primi a votare a Gerusalemme insieme alla compagna Michal Herzog. A Tel Aviv anche nel giorno delle urne i familiari degli ostaggi si sono riuniti per esortare gli israeliani a votare "per il cambiamento, la giustizia e un futuro migliore". Lo riportano i media israeliani. Anche alcuni leader di partito hanno già espresso le loroe preferenze. Il ministro di estrema destra Bezalel Smotrich, presidente del Sionismo Religioso, ha votato nell'insediamento di Kedumin, in Cisgiordania, esortando gli elettori a mobilitare amici e familiari affinché si rechino alle urne e "si assumano la responsabilità dello Stato di Israele, l'unico Stato ebraico". Yair Golan, leader dei Democratici, ha votato a Rosh Ha'ayin. "Oggi è il giorno in cui salviamo Israele. Abbiamo combattuto per quattro anni nelle strade e ora ci rivolgiamo alle urne", ha dichiarato Golan. Anche il ministro della sicurezza di estrema destra Itamar Ben-Gvir ha votato in un insediamento israeliano in Cisgiordania.

07:46

Aperti i seggi per il rinnovo della Knesset

Si sono aperti alle 7 locali (le 6 in Italia) i seggi per la formazione della 26ma Knesset. Si tratta della prima votazione dall'attentato del 7 ottobre. Sono circa 7 milioni e 331 mila gli israeliani chiamati alle urne oggi fino alle 22 locali (le 21 in Italia). In lizza ci sono 36 partiti, di cui solo 13 vengono rilevati nei sondaggi perché superano la soglia di sbarramento al 3,25%.

Gli exit poll verranno annunciati immediatamente con la chiusura delle urne, ma i risultati finali saranno ufficializzati solo otto giorni dopo il voto, il 4 novembre. Il conteggio delle 'buste doppie' - ossia di chi vota lontano dal proprio luogo di residenza, come soldati, diplomatici, persone ospedalizzate - richiede più tempo e in passato ha ribaltato i risultati emersi dagli exit poll iniziali.

In un sistema proporzionale puro a collegio unico, determinante per la distribuzione dei 120 seggi della Knesset è l'affluenza al voto che quest'anno, nelle prime elezioni dopo tre anni di guerra, è prevista essere particolarmente alta: i sondaggisti rilevano che il 74% della popolazione ha espresso la volontà di andare a votare. Alle ultime elezioni del 2022 l'affluenza fu del 70%. I partiti più quotati alla vigilia sono il Likud, del premier in carica Benjamin Netanyahu (il più longevo sella storia del Paese), e Yashar! articles.body:
Exit polls are expected soon after voting closes late on Tuesday, but a final verdict might take days.

Israelis are voting in a closely watched election to decide on the direction of the country, three years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on southern Israel that set off the genocidal war on Gaza.

The first election since those attacks comes at a time when Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of its neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

- list 1 of 3UN panel accuses Israel of ‘extermination’ in West Bank, genocide in Gaza

- list 2 of 3‘Everything destroyed’: Hebron businesses count cost of Israeli assault

- list 3 of 3Could the midterms change US military support for Israel?

But the vote also comes amid growing domestic questions that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces over alleged failures that allowed the October 7 attack, his government’s handling of efforts to retrieve captives taken to Gaza, alleged corruption and disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service.

In final polls published Friday, Netanyahu’s coalition is expected to be neck and neck with – or trail slightly behind – the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.

According to Israeli news outlet Haaretz, which has collated polls from Israeli news channels, as of Friday, an average of Channels 11, 12 and 13 predicts Netanyahu’s bloc will win 50 seats while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc will take 54 seats. The Israeli parliament, known as the Knesset, has 120 seats in all, so 61 is the mark that a grouping needs to reach a majority.

Here’s what you need to know about the election.

When do polls close in Israel?

On Tuesday, polls opened at 7am local time (05:00 GMT) and will end at 10pm (20:00 GMT).

About 7.3 million Israelis will be eligible to vote, including 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel. Israelis living abroad cannot vote because the country does not have a general absentee ballot, requiring voters to be physically present on election day.

Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception and cast their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.

When will Israel’s election results be announced?

News channels will broadcast exit poll results once the election ends, with the first indications likely within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or weeks to get a clear result.

Results will also be live on the Central Elections Committee website once polls close.

While a clear picture of the election results may come out quickly, if no party or coalition secures a majority, it could take much longer.

The final vote tally is expected by Friday, and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.

How does the electoral system work?

Under a proportional representation system, Israelis vote for a single party, not individual candidates.

The number of seats the party gains in the Knesset is linked to the proportion of the vote it receives. For example, if Netanyahu’s Likud party secures 50 percent of the national vote, it would take 50 percent of the Knesset’s 120 seats.

A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats.

For a party to enter the Knesset, it must secure at least 3.25 percent of the national vote.

About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.

How is Israel’s next prime minister chosen?

Once the final count is in, President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.

The person nominated then has up to 42 days to form a government. As it stands, no single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks.

What happens if Netanyahu or his rivals cannot form a government?

If no government emerges, the current cabinet, Netanyahu’s government, will remain as a caretaker government.

But before that point, whoever gains the most votes will have different options to assemble support from smaller parties, including forming a minority government or working with another political leader to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.

If all negotiations fail, and no grouping is able to cobble together a workable government, new elections will have to be called.

articles.title: Palestine weekly: West Bank under siege as Israelis go to the polls
articles.summary: Israel sealed the West Bank, emptied parts of Hebron and tightened the squeeze on Gaza as its election campaign closed.
articles.preview: Israel sealed the West Bank, emptied parts of Hebron and tightened the squeeze on Gaza as its election campaign wrapped up. While Israelis go to the polls this week in one of the most consequential elections in years, many Palestinians in the West Bank have been confined to their homes or neighbourhoods as a wave of Israeli military operations around Hebron continues.
articles.body:
Israel sealed the West Bank, emptied parts of Hebron and tightened the squeeze on Gaza as its election campaign wrapped up.

While Israelis go to the polls this week in one of the most consequential elections in years, many Palestinians in the West Bank have been confined to their homes or neighbourhoods as a wave of Israeli military operations around Hebron continues.

The West Bank city has been in a state of lockdown since two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at an army checkpoint at Hebron’s northern entrance on Friday, killing two Israeli soldiers and wounding three. After the suspects were killed, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the isolation of Hebron and said troops would go house to house in the gunmen’s neighbourhood. “We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he proclaimed.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

- list 1 of 3Could the midterms change US military support for Israel?

- list 2 of 3UN panel accuses Israel of ‘extermination’ in West Bank, genocide in Gaza

- list 3 of 3‘Everything destroyed’: Hebron businesses count cost of Israeli assault

What followed has been a mass displacement operation in the Hebron area, echoing last year’s military expulsions of three refugee camps, alongside widespread destruction in the neighbourhoods targeted by the army, evoking scenes out of Gaza.

During the weekend, soldiers ordered residents of al-Jalda and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods out by loudspeaker, according to residents. Thousands have been forced out of their homes already, with Defence Minister Israel Katz saying people would not be allowed back “until we’ve finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron”. By Monday, the governorate’s fourth day under closure, at least 3,171 Palestinians from 488 families had been forced out, according to Hebron Municipality data cited by the Wafa news agency. Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin said Israeli forces had searched more than 500 homes, arrested more than 70 people and fragmented the city with 128 closed gates and 120 checkpoints.

The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society says the displaced include 127 infants, 81 pregnant women and 26 people with disabilities, and that at least 47 people have been detained in Hebron since Friday.

Bulldozers razed a three-apartment building belonging to Riyad Amrish, as well as a tile and ceramics factory, an auto-parts shop and other businesses in Farsh al-Hawa. Israel’s Channel 12 said Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich ordered the demolitions.

Israeli NGO B’Tselem warned the operation amounts to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.

Sieges at every scale

But Hebron is only the most prominent of multiple sieges happening at different scales, with years-long efforts to strategically encircle Palestinian communities in the West Bank now being employed to devastating effect:

- Homes: The three-week siege by Israeli settlers of the family of Yusuf Shanaran in Wadi al-Rakheem, Masafer Yatta continues, with the family unable to leave or receive aid for days at a time without army coordination, Shanaran told Al Jazeera on Monday. In Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, village Mayor Marwan Sabah said Mohammad al-Obaiyat’s 1954 house received a demolition order with a November 11 deadline after months with a gate blocking its road. Settlers have since been filmed attempting to break into the family home, which has been besieged for nearly a month, with few supplies entering during that time.

- A village: Madama, south of Nablus, is only just emerging from a two-week siege of its four entrances, with heavy restrictions remaining at its just-opened northern entrance, according to villagers. A kindergarten principal there told Al Jazeera she lifts children over the barrier one by one.

- A region: Twelve Masafer Yatta communities in the southern West Bank were cut off for several days, with about 50 teachers unable to reach their schools, and Wafa reported that Bethlehem governorate’s roads were closed for several days.

- A territory: The Israeli army barred Palestinian workers from illegal Israeli settlements on Sunday and Monday and will close all crossings on election day.

The only Palestinians who can vote – Palestinian citizens of Israel – may face issues at the polls, too; Israel’s Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu’s Likud party was preparing to challenge results from Arab polling stations before a vote had been cast.

Olive harvest attacks

This year’s olive harvest has drawn unprecedented levels of settler pogroms, theft and closed-military-zone orders. The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission has counted 482 attacks on the harvest by Sunday across nine governorates, Wafa reported.

At the same time, Israel released nine of 10 settlers arrested following last week’s attacks on a foreign journalist and diplomats. The attacks have continued undeterred. Wafa reported 17 attacks on farmers and their property on Thursday, and the commission documented 21 in 12 hours on Friday. The past week’s harvest-related incidents fall into a handful of repeating patterns:

- Theft of olives and equipment in at least a dozen villages, including Sinjil, Silwad, Berin, Beit Iksa, al-Lubban Asharqiya, Kafr Malek, Ein Arik and Deir Ballut, according to Wafa and local reports. Near Immatin, at least 25 masked settlers sent three tractors and two trailers rolling down a hillside, destroying the equipment and olives on board.

- Assaults in at least 15 places, among them Burin, where stones left three farmers with head wounds; Ein Arik, where The Times of Israel reported a farmer suffered fractures; and Beit Iksa, al-Lubban Asharqiya and Kafr Malek, where pickers were pepper-sprayed. Settlers fired live rounds at pickers in Berin and Osarin, and smashed cars and trucks in Marda, Wad Qaddoum and Sinjil, Wafa and local monitors reported.

- Detentions and expulsions in at least a dozen places. Fifteen farmers were detained in as-Sawiya on Sunday. In Beit Iksa, where the harvest had been coordinated with the Israeli Civil Administration, Mohammed al-Kiswani was pepper-sprayed and detained; settlers told farmers they would never harvest “with or without coordination”. Land at Deir Jarir and Turmus Aya was declared a closed military zone without orders shown, Ayed Jafry reported – and far-right influencers were brought to film the expulsions for campaign content.

- Damage to olive trees in at least 10 locations. Settlers burned dozens of trees in Burqa on Friday, keeping Palestinian Civil Defence crews out, according to Wafa; trees were set on fire in Immatin, Salem and Beit Furik; and a bulldozer uprooted hundreds in Madama, according to villagers. Soldiers uprooted dozens more in Deir Qaddis for a settler road and posted a notice at al-Mughayyir ordering hundreds of trees uprooted and in Khirbet Abu Falah for a “security buffer zone”, giving residents 24 hours to object, Jafry reported.

- Arson. In Burqa, settlers set fire on Tuesday to a memorial to Palestinian residents killed and, an hour later, to the home of Jamal Bajes, a Palestinian-American – the second arson at his house in recent months, according to local reports. Local activist networks reported a home was burned in Deir Abu Mishal, and Wafa said settlers tried to set another ablaze in Burin under army protection.

Those joining the harvests in solidarity were targeted, too. United States Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was among about 80 volunteers detained near Nahalin on Wednesday and released with a “warning”; Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused him of “harvesting headlines”.

Gaza: Managed scarcity as killings continue

The last week in Gaza saw at least 37 more Palestinians killed as Israel’s daily attacks continued. Monday’s daily report from the Gaza Ministry of Health alone recorded 11 deaths – eight newly killed, three recovered from rubble – and 35 wounded, taking the toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,559 killed and 5,608 wounded, with a cumulative toll of 74,555.

Among those killed this week:

- Akram Yassin and his wife, Dina Abu Bakr, in a strike on their apartment behind al-Shifa Hospital on Tuesday.

- Majdi Mohammad Fakhri Hassan, a child, shot near the Happy City resort south of Khan Younis; Rafif Raed Lubad, 17, shot in the head in Jabalia; and Fatima Abu Laban, killed in Tal al-Dhahab, northwest of Beit Lahiya on Saturday, according to Wafa.

- Three security guards – Sami Baroud, Ashraf Dahlan and Shadi Abu Ataya – at the Islamic University in Gaza City on Sunday, after an earlier strike wounded seven students. Israel said it was targeting a Hamas operative.

For days, hunger worsened with crossings into Gaza shut: Flour stocks ran out, leaving seven of 20 commercial bakeries open, Abdul Nasser al-Ajrami of the bakers’ association told Wafa, and a tray of eggs reached a price of 60 shekels ($19.50).

The pressure began to ease somewhat on the evening of October 23, as Israel told traders that commercial goods would resume and an Egyptian committee delivered flour, Mohammad Abu Warda of the private sector’s emergency committee said.

articles.title: Postres variados
articles.summary: En un menú gastronómico o en unas elecciones como las de Israel, la libertad de elegir importa incluso cuando ninguna opción resulta apetecible
articles.preview: Las comidas y cenas que solía hacer mi madre cada día para mis hermanos y para mí cuando éramos niños tenían la estructura de un buen relato: empezaban con los clásicos —ensalada, patatas, arroz, guisantes— y siempre dejaban el final abierto, justo en el momento en el que el protagonista tenía que escoger. No teníamos voz ni voto en el plato principal, pero sabíamos que al terminar la comida siempre había “postres variados”, una expresión que mi madre debía de haber oído en alguna boda o en el bufé de un hotel.
articles.body:
Las comidas y cenas que solía hacer mi madre cada día para mis hermanos y para mí cuando éramos niños tenían la estructura de un buen relato: empezaban con los clásicos —ensalada, patatas, arroz, guisantes— y siempre dejaban el final abierto, justo en el momento en el que el protagonista tenía que escoger. No teníamos voz ni voto en el plato principal, pero sabíamos que al terminar la comida siempre había “postres variados”, una expresión que mi madre debía de haber oído en alguna boda o en el bufé de un hotel.

Dado que, de niña, ella había pasado hambre, primero en un gueto y luego en los austeros orfanatos de Polonia y Francia, me es difícil imaginar que, en aquellos años, hubiera podido decidir algún día qué comer. Quizá precisamente por eso quería que sus hijos sí tuvieran ese privilegio: la libertad de elegir. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: Salvini rieletto segretario della Lega, nel simbolo arriva ‘Italia Federale’
articles.summary: AGI - Matteo Salvini viene confermato, per la quarta volta, alla guida della Lega e già cambia il simbolo del partito, come pure era filtrato negli scorsi giorni, eliminando il proprio nome dal logo, sostituito dalla dicitura ‘Italia Federale’. Poi rilancia sugli aiuti a Kiev: “Non possiamo continuare a mandare soldi e armi all’Ucraina”. Una posizione, ha spiegato Salvini, che il vicepremier porterà al tavolo del prossimo Consiglio dei ministri. Nel racconto dell’ultima giornata del congresso straordinario del partito fondato da Umberto Bossi è inevitabile partire dai titoli di coda, dunque dai numeri. Il voto: 465 preferenze contro 146 Alla fine, nonostante i rilievi dei delegati dello sfidante Massimo Garavaglia sul pericolo di schede ‘segnalate’ e possibili foto al seggio per dimostrare la preferenza, si vota a cabina chiusa e il pallottoliere segna 465 voti per Salvini e 146 per l’ex ministro del Turismo. 76% per il vicepremier, quasi 24% per Garavaglia. Un risultato abbastanza in linea con le aspettative della vigilia, che fa dire al capogruppo al Senato Massimiliano Romeo, ieri tra i più critici nei confronti di Salvini, che esisteva un “disagio reale, non solo lombardo”. Il discorso del segretario rieletto Dopo la proclamazione e un abbraccio sul palco con l’avversario, il segretario rieletto allontana i retroscena su possibili “epurazioni” e promette che “sarà intransigente con chi non versa i soldi al partito”. Poi scalda la platea, che lo aveva accolto con il coro ‘Matteo, Matteo’ e una serie di striscioni, tra cui uno che si augurava un suo ritorno al Viminale, dicendo che “la sera delle elezioni Giorgia Meloni tornerà presidente del Consiglio e Lega Italia Federale sarà secondo partito coalizione, per il momento”. Il nuovo simbolo: ‘Italia Federale’ al posto di ‘Salvini premier’ Sì, perché la Lega non avrà più, nel suo simbolo, la dicitura ‘Salvini premier’, sostituita da ‘Italia Federale’. Uno sguardo al futuro in vista delle prossime elezioni politiche, ma anche una citazione del passato, rivendicata dallo stesso Salvini quando ha mostrato sul palco dell’Allianz MiCo il contrassegno con l’Alberto da Giussano e la scritta ‘Italia Federale’ con cui la Lega si presentò al Sud e nel Lazio dal 1993 al 1995, sotto la guida di Bossi. E il vicepremier, nel suo intervento, per rispondere a chi lo aveva accusato di portare la Lega verso l’estrema destra, tradendo la storia del partito, mostra una serie di manifesti del Carroccio delle stagioni del passato. Salvini sostiene che, anche in altre fasi della sua parabola, la Lega non ha mai rinunciato ai toni forti e fa vedere il manifesto forse più noto, quello sull’immigrazione con l’indiano d’America. “Loro non hanno potuto mettere regole all’immigrazione, ora vivono nelle riserve”, si legge, accanto all’immagine di un nativo. Il dibattito sulla collocazione del partito Il dibattito sulla collocazione del partito nello spettro politico ha fatto da filo conduttore della giornata di oggi. La vicesegretaria Silvia Sardone è netta: “Ho sentito che siamo né di destra né di sinistra, io non sono mai stata e mai sarò comunista”. Con lei il ministro Giuseppe Valditara: “Sono anticomunista da sempre, mai a sinistra”. Nel suo intervento, Garavaglia delinea un posizionamento diverso: “‘Né neri né rossi, ma liberi con Bossi’ scandiva Salvini guidando il corteo dei giovani padani, la Lega non è né a destra né a sinistra”. La ‘sintesi’ la fa il ministro Giancarlo Giorgetti. “Io credevo e credo nella Lega nazionale ma non credo nella Lega nazionalista, credo nella Lega delle identità che è quello che ci distingue dall’omologazione”, dice il ministro dell’Economia, definendosi “conservatore”. L’appello identitario contro l’avversario dell’”omologazione” riecheggia anche nelle parole del presidente della Camera Lorenzo Fontana, che rimarca: “Non voglio che si muoia fotocopie”. Il “tradimento” di Vannacci fa da sfondo anche nella giornata di oggi. “Noi abbiamo comprato un giocatore, non ha funzionato”, ricorda Garavaglia, che invita a “pescare dal vivaio”. “Qualcuno fa chiacchiere, noi facciamo le cose”, è l’opinione di Salvini a proposito del leader di Futuro Nazionale. Garavaglia, come aveva fatto Romeo ieri, sottolinea che “l’obiettivo è invertire il trend” e “dobbiamo svegliarci”. Da Salvini la sferzata agli alleati, a cui “chiediamo il rispetto delle nostre posizioni”, perché “nelle regioni dove siamo in maggioranza non tollererò più che la Lega sia trattata come un alleato di serie B”. Tra le posizioni, quella sull’Ucraina, con Salvini pronto “a portare in Cdm” lo stop a “armi e soldi” a Kiev. Sul fronte-Lega, invece, c’è da mettere a punto il cronoprogramma dei prossimi passaggi. A partire dal varo della nuova segreteria politica, per cui “bisognerà aspettare una o due settimane”, spiega Salvini. Che aggiunge: “Mi hanno dato mandato di istituire questa segretaria che dovrà coinvolgere tutti i territori, le correnti le lasciamo alla Schlein e al Pd”. Mentre, sulle candidature, dice che sarà scelto “chi ha consenso”. Tempi rapidi anche per l’approvazione del nuovo simbolo, che dovrà passare da una riunione del Consiglio Federale da convocare a stretto giro.

Una posizione, ha spiegato Salvini, che il vicepremier porterà al tavolo del prossimo Consiglio dei ministri.

Nel racconto dell’ultima giornata del congresso straordinario del partito fondato da Umberto Bossi è inevitabile partire dai titoli di coda, dunque dai numeri. Il voto: 465 preferenze contro 146 Alla fine, nonostante i rilievi dei delegati dello sfidante Massimo Garavaglia sul pericolo di schede ‘segnalate’ e possibili foto al seggio per dimostrare la preferenza, si vota a cabina chiusa e il pallottoliere segna 465 voti per Salvini e 146 per l’ex ministro del Turismo.

76% per il vicepremier, quasi 24% per Garavaglia. Un risultato abbastanza in linea con le aspettative della vigilia, che fa dire al capogruppo al Senato Massimiliano Romeo, ieri tra i più critici nei confronti di Salvini, che esisteva un “disagio reale, non solo lombardo”. Il discorso del segretario rieletto Dopo la proclamazione e un abbraccio sul palco con l’avversario, il segretario rieletto allontana i retroscena su possibili “epurazioni” e promette che “sarà intransigente con chi non versa i soldi al partito”.

Poi scalda la platea, che lo aveva accolto con il coro ‘Matteo, Matteo’ e una serie di striscioni, tra cui uno che si augurava un suo ritorno al Viminale, dicendo che “la sera delle elezioni Giorgia Meloni tornerà presidente del Consiglio e Lega Italia Federale sarà secondo partito coalizione, per il momento”. Il nuovo simbolo: ‘Italia Federale’ al posto di ‘Salvini premier’ Sì, perché la Lega non avrà più, nel suo simbolo, la dicitura ‘Salvini premier’, sostituita da ‘Italia Federale’.

Uno sguardo al futuro in vista delle prossime elezioni politiche, ma anche una citazione del passato, rivendicata dallo stesso Salvini quando ha mostrato sul palco dell’Allianz MiCo il contrassegno con l’Alberto da Giussano e la scritta ‘Italia Federale’ con cui la Lega si presentò al Sud e nel Lazio dal 1993 al 1995, sotto la guida di Bossi. E il vicepremier, nel suo intervento, per rispondere a chi lo aveva accusato di portare la Lega verso l’estrema destra, tradendo la storia del partito, mostra una serie di manifesti del Carroccio delle stagioni del passato.

Salvini sostiene che, anche in altre fasi della sua parabola, la Lega non ha mai rinunciato ai toni forti e fa vedere il manifesto forse più noto, quello sull’immigrazione con l’indiano d’America. “Loro non hanno potuto mettere regole all’immigrazione, ora vivono nelle riserve”, si legge, accanto all’immagine di un nativo. Il dibattito sulla collocazione del partito Il dibattito sulla collocazione del partito nello spettro politico ha fatto da filo conduttore della giornata di oggi.

La vicesegretaria Silvia Sardone è netta: “Ho sentito che siamo né di destra né di sinistra, io non sono mai stata e mai sarò comunista”. Con lei il ministro Giuseppe Valditara: “Sono anticomunista da sempre, mai a sinistra”. Nel suo intervento, Garavaglia delinea un posizionamento diverso: “‘Né neri né rossi, ma liberi con Bossi’ scandiva Salvini guidando il corteo dei giovani padani, la Lega non è né a destra né a sinistra”.

La ‘sintesi’ la fa il ministro Giancarlo Giorgetti. “Io credevo e credo nella Lega nazionale ma non credo nella Lega nazionalista, credo nella Lega delle identità che è quello che ci distingue dall’omologazione”, dice il ministro dell’Economia, definendosi “conservatore”. L’appello identitario contro l’avversario dell’”omologazione” riecheggia anche nelle parole del presidente della Camera Lorenzo Fontana, che rimarca: “Non voglio che si muoia fotocopie”.

Il “tradimento” di Vannacci fa da sfondo anche nella giornata di oggi. “Noi abbiamo comprato un giocatore, non ha funzionato”, ricorda Garavaglia, che invita a “pescare dal vivaio”. “Qualcuno fa chiacchiere, noi facciamo le cose”, è l’opinione di Salvini a proposito del leader di Futuro Nazionale. Garavaglia, come aveva fatto Romeo ieri, sottolinea che “l’obiettivo è invertire il trend” e “dobbiamo svegliarci”.

Da Salvini la sferzata agli alleati, a cui “chiediamo il rispetto delle nostre posizioni”, perché “nelle regioni dove siamo in maggioranza non tollererò più che la Lega sia trattata come un alleato di serie B”. Tra le posizioni, quella sull’Ucraina, con Salvini pronto “a portare in Cdm” lo stop a “armi e soldi” a Kiev. Sul fronte-Lega, invece, c’è da mettere a punto il cronoprogramma dei prossimi passaggi.

A partire dal varo della nuova segreteria politica, per cui “bisognerà aspettare una o due settimane”, spiega Salvini. Che aggiunge: “Mi hanno dato mandato di istituire questa segretaria che dovrà coinvolgere tutti i territori, le correnti le lasciamo alla Schlein e al Pd”. Mentre, sulle candidature, dice che sarà scelto “chi ha consenso”. Tempi rapidi anche per l’approvazione del nuovo simbolo, che dovrà passare da una riunione del Consiglio Federale da convocare a stretto giro.

articles.title: L’estrema destra sta capitalizzando sui disordini in Francia e Italia
articles.summary: Online le narrazioni xenofobe di “guerra etnica” o “assalto all’Occidente” sono sempre più sdoganate
articles.preview: Il 19 ottobre 2026 il noto streamer statunitense e commentatore politico Zack Hoyt (conosciuto con il nome di “Asmongold”), 3,5 milioni di follower su Twitch, ha fatto una diretta in cui reagisce e commenta mentre guarda alcuni filmati dei disordini avvenuti tra il 17 e il 18 ottobre in varie città italiane nel corso delle manifestazioni contro il carovita. Pubblicato poi su YouTube col titolo “What the f**k is happening in Italy??” (“Che ca**o sta succedendo in Italia??”), il video ha già totalizzato quasi 1,7 milioni di visualizzazioni.
articles.body:
Il 19 ottobre 2026 il noto streamer statunitense e commentatore politico Zack Hoyt (conosciuto con il nome di “Asmongold”), 3,5 milioni di follower su Twitch, ha fatto una diretta in cui reagisce e commenta mentre guarda alcuni filmati dei disordini avvenuti tra il 17 e il 18 ottobre in varie città italiane nel corso delle manifestazioni contro il carovita. Pubblicato poi su YouTube col titolo “What the f**k is happening in Italy??” (“Che ca**o sta succedendo in Italia??”), il video ha già totalizzato quasi 1,7 milioni di visualizzazioni. Affermatosi inizialmente come streamer del videogioco World of Warcraft, col tempo Hoyt ha attirato un pubblico molto vasto che lo segue per ascoltare le sue opinioni, orientate verso l’estrema destra.

Per mezz’ora Hoyt mostra video di saccheggi e vandalismi di ogni genere, e risponde ai messaggi che arrivano in diretta. Secondo Hoyt l’Italia si troverebbe in una situazione apocalittica, sull’orlo di una guerra civile portata avanti da un corpo estraneo alla società italiana, impegnato a distruggerne lo stile di vita. Quando qualche follower accenna alla precarietà generazionale e alle disparità di classe, una delle chiavi di lettura con cui analisti ed economisti stanno provando a spiegare dati alla mano le ragioni di tanta rabbia, Hoyt è categorico: «non ci dovrebbe essere disparità di classe, perché queste persone non dovrebbero nemmeno stare a casa nostra». La soluzione? Hoyt invoca contro i partecipanti ai disordini un approccio simile a quello duro e autoritario con cui il presidente del Salvador Nayib Bukele, popolarissimo negli ambienti della destra internazionale, ha combattuto le gang criminali del suo Paese – un approccio suggerito da Bukele stesso.

Il video di Hoyt rappresenta perfettamente il modo con cui l’estrema destra internazionale sta provando a raccontare i riots avvenuti in varie città italiane e francesi il 17 e il 18 ottobre: una crisi esistenziale dell’Occidente, la prova che il multiculturalismo ha fallito e la necessità di salvare le nostre società dai cittadini con background migratorio o di seconda generazione, eventualmente «remigrandoli tutti». Tuttavia, Hoyt non sembra costruire questa narrazione da solo. Durante la diretta, mentre lo streamer passa da un video all’altro, si intravede una lista dei link che sta seguendo, che è uno spaccato dei canali che in questi giorni hanno contribuito di più a diffondere una narrazione etno-nazionalista, scatenare panico e diffondere odio.

La rete di account di estrema destra

Da quando l’allora Twitter è stato acquistato, nel 2022, da Elon Musk, oltre al cambio del nome in X, la piattaforma social ha ridotto drasticamente la moderazione dei contenuti e si è trasformata in megafono dell’estrema destra. Non è un caso che tutti i link nella lista rimandano a X. Compare l’aggregatore di notizie polacco xenofobo e ultraconservatore Visegrad24, noto per diffondere disinformazione su svariati temi, un cui post sull’incendio del Municipio di Limoges è stato ripreso anche dal vice-presidente statunitense JD Vance; un video con più di 14 milioni di visualizzazioni di un account di propaganda MAGA e anti-immigrazione secondo cui un cittadino italiano, esasperato dalla situazione, ha affrontato da solo i saccheggiatori – in realtà analizzando il video Facta ha identificato l’uomo in un carabiniere in borghese.

Nella dieta mediatica di Hoyt spiccano anche due account italiani: uno è @FantomasRitorna, un profilo italiano di estrema destra attivo da diversi anni, che nonostante un seguito tutto sommato marginale, ha postato in questi giorni video dei saccheggi che hanno raccolto singolarmente più di sette milioni di visualizzazioni. L’altro è Radio Genoa, un account italiano in lingua inglese che in questi anni si è affermato a livello internazionale come uno dei più noti divulgatori di messaggi d’odio, razzismo, islamofobia e disinformazione a tema immigrazione. Con i disordini in Francia e in Italia, Radio Genoa sta avendo un ruolo importante nell’amplificare questa visione apocalittica. Solo per fare alcuni esempi, nei tweet che accompagnano i video degli ultimi giorni Radio Genoa scrive che “l’Europa è nel caos totale”, “questa Francia non ha futuro” e “Milano è perduta”.

Radio Genoa ha anche spinto e diffuso l’idea che dietro gli scontri ci sia una matrice religiosa: in un video che ha quasi cinque milioni di visualizzazioni su X, si vede un oggetto in fiamme in una strada antistante il Duomo di Milano, con la chiesa sullo sfondo distante centinaia di metri. Ma il commento è il seguente: «L’Italia come la Francia. Davanti al Duomo di Milano. Un simbolo della cristianità sotto assedio  Questa è una guerra alla nostra storia, alla nostra cultura, alle nostre tradizioni e alla nostra identità». In un altro post scrive che i cristiani sono sotto attacco ovunque, per poi aggiungere: «Questi criminali – nordafricani – hanno preso di mira il duomo di Milano. Il video lo mostra chiaramente». In realtà il video mostra un ragazzo che passa in una via laterale del Duomo di Milano mentre spruzza in aria il contenuto di un estintore.

Radio Genoa non è nuova a diffondere contenuti falsi, decontestualizzati o fuorvianti, ma la frequenza con cui l’ha fatto in questi giorni è notevole: oltre ai video già citati, in cui il Duomo sarebbe stato assediato da manifestanti islamisti, l’account ha diffuso molto altro materiale teso a seminare panico nell’opinione pubblica. Un video del 18 ottobre creato con l’intelligenza artificiale mostra la mostra la Torre Eiffel in fiamme, con il testo: «Parigi, molto, molto presto».

Su chi gestisce Radio Genoa fino a qualche anno fa non si sapeva molto, anche se un’indagine di Facta del 2023 aveva permesso di aggiungere qualche dettaglio importante. Nel 2024 anche il programma televisivo di giornalismo investigativo olandese Pointer si era messo sulle sue tracce, attirato dal fatto che il politico di estrema destra Geert Wilders condividesse frequentemente i contenuti dell’account. L’inchiesta aveva ricondotto il profilo su X a una persona, originaria della Liguria, chiamata Antonio Mastantuono. Lo stesso Mastantuono è successivamente venuto allo scoperto nel 2024, rivelando di essere oggetto di un’indagine da parte della magistratura italiana per incitamento all’odio, ottenendo per questo la solidarietà del senatore della Lega Claudio Borghi.

Da allora l’account è cresciuto, e la sua influenza come canale di propaganda anti-immigrazione è diventata evidente. Qualche giorno fa l’account X di Radio Genoa ha annunciato di aver raddoppiato con un nuovo sito. Allo stesso tempo, ha chiarito che «in segno di rispetto per @ElonMusk, che ci ha restituito la libertà di parola, @RadioGenoa non aprirà mai profili su Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube o Telegram.  Finché Elon proteggerà la libertà di parola, resteremo al 100% su X. La lealtà conta».

Intanto sui social continua a rimbalzare questa realtà parallela: stando a un video su X da 1,8 milioni di visualizzazioni postato da un account sudamericano di destra la città di Bologna «è stata completamente devastata». Altri account, condividendo le stesse immagini, hanno rincarato dicendo che «Bologna ha vissuto una delle peggiori notti della sua vita», o è «diventata una zona di guerra». In realtà a Bologna gli scontri con la polizia sono avvenuti quasi esclusivamente nell’area circostante la stazione ferroviaria.

La strumentalizzazione delle proteste francesi

In Francia, dove da tempo attivisti e politici di estrema destra sono riusciti a trovare spazio all’interno dei media mainstream, i movimenti estremisti stanno sfruttando l’occasione per spostare ancora di più il confine del dicibile, e raccontare ciò che è successo nei giorni passati come una guerra etnica. Il caso più evidente è quello della giovane attivista di estrema destra Thaïs d’Escufon, i cui video stanno circolando molto online, al punto che il senatore repubblicao Ted Cruz ne ha condiviso uno con i suoi sette milioni di follower. «L’unica soluzione pacifica è rimandarli nei loro Paesi d’origine che amano così tanto. Non possiamo coesistere. Saremo noi, o loro», ha detto l’attivista. D’Escufon è stata la portavoce del gruppo suprematista Génération identitaire dal 2018 fino al suo scioglimento da parte del governo francese nel 2021. Génération identitaire aveva ricevuto in passato delle donazioni anche da Brenton Tarrant, il terrorista responsabile dell’attentato nella Moschea di Christchurch in Nuova Zelanda, costato la vita a 51 persone. Eppure un profilo come il suo, che chiede apertamente l’uccisione dei manifestanti, sta scalando la piramide mediatica e trovando casse di risonanza sempre più vaste.

In questi giorni le proteste sono state sfruttate anche a fini politici attraverso un ampio ricorso all’intelligenza artificiale, usata per creare contenuti di disinformazione di grande impatto. Il caso più noto è la falsa foto di due ottantenni derubati dai manifestanti, resa virale da un profilo su X che in passato aveva già diffuso disinformazione contro attivisti per la Palestina e il partito di estrema sinistra La France Insoumise.

Il presidente francese Emmanuel Macron intanto ha condannato la strumentalizzazione della situazione francese, affermando che «alcuni leader, «nel pieno delle campagne elettorali, sia qui nella regione sia dall’altra parte dell’Atlantico  stanno usando il nostro Paese per le loro campagne politiche». Macron ha anche denunciato la circolazione di immagini generate dall’intelligenza artificiale «che raffigurano scene che in realtà non sono mai accadute in Francia. C’è stato chi ha sostenuto che fossimo stati invasi da orde di migranti e islamisti, cosa assolutamente falsa». In molti hanno subito pensato alle parole del presidente statunitense Donald Trump, che qualche giorno prima aveva commentato che «se l’Europa non chiude i suoi confini e non ne espelle i criminali, come le persone che stanno protestando, l’Europa è finita».

Tuttavia, prese di posizione analoghe sono arrivate sui social anche dal premier polacco Donald Tusk e il primo ministro ungherese Péter Magyar: commentando le immagini provenienti da Parigi, entrambi hanno parlato della necessità di confini sicuri e della difesa dell’Europa dall’immigrazione illegale. È la prova che la narrazione identitaria e xenofoba sulle proteste è ormai riuscita a far breccia anche tra i leader conservatori meno radicali.

articles.body:
If there’s one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it’s data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities — and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them — has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns.

Some midterm races come down to ‘people who hate data centers’ versus ‘people who hate them even more.’

At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that says it supports AI safeguards, says it’s raised $80 million. Both have funded Democratic and Republican-aligned groups. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies, like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety.

All sorts of candidates appear to be distancing themselves from data centers and taking steps to assuage voters’ concerns about unconstrained buildouts in their backyards. How far they’re willing to go — including by backing an outright moratorium on development — varies. While many Democratic candidates seem likelier to back a pause, that’s not always the case. And though some Republicans have leaned on party messaging about putting development in local control, rather than supporting a ban, others say a pause is exactly what the moment calls for.

Texas gubernatorial and Senate races

Deep red Texas has the second-highest number of planned data center projects in the country after Virginia, and across multiple races, data centers have emerged as a key wedge issue. Democratic and Republican candidates are all trying to look tough on data centers but emphasize different messages in their plans. For example, in the Senate race, Democratic candidate and State Rep. James Talarico includes references to environmental impact and sharing corporate profit with the public, while Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton discusses the need to keep Chinese technology out of US data centers. Both, however, want data centers to bear their own energy infrastructure-related costs and want to do away with certain tax exemptions for them.

In July, Talarico unveiled his “Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan,” which would end state sales tax incentives, give communities more of a say in data center development, require a closed-loop water system in new data centers to limit consumption, and create federal standards to protect the energy grid and environment. Talarico has also proposed an “AI Dividend” for Americans that would be funded by a tax on “AI-attributable profits.”

For his part, Paxton’s “Texas First Data Center Plan,” unveiled in August, would support Gov. Greg Abbott’s state-level policies, including repealing sales tax exemptions for data centers, requiring them to pay for electricity they use and add to state capacity, and preventing AI data centers from building in rural parts of the state. On the federal level, Paxton says he would co-sponsor an existing bill making it easier for data centers to connect to off-grid power systems, introduce new legislation prohibiting the use of Chinese technology to power US data centers or infrastructure, and hold data center companies criminally liable if the facility “empowers AI chatbots that undermine children’s safety.”

Talarico has also proposed an “AI Dividend” for Americans that would be funded by a tax on “AI-attributable profits”

In the race for the governor’s office, Democratic challenger and State Rep. Gina Hinojosa has accused Abbott, the Republican incumbent, of “flip-flopping” on data centers. Abbott’s office put out a press release last year celebrating a $40 billion Google investment that would include three new data center campuses, but in August 2026, with campaign season heating up, he announced an audit that could slow new facilities connecting to the state energy grid. Hinojosa, who has recently called for a statewide moratorium on data center development, pounced on the perceived inconsistency. “Greg Abbott has zero credibility here. Nobody believes that the arsonist is about to put out the fire,” she said in a social media video.

The outcome of these races remains highly uncertain. Cook Political Report changed its rating for the governor’s race earlier this month from a likely Republican win to one that leans Republican. It says the open field for the Senate race is a toss-up.

Florida gubernatorial race

In Florida, there’s a clash over whether large-scale data centers can be reined in with the right policies or if they should be outright barred in the state. Democratic candidate and former congressman David Jolly has pledged to install a one-year ban on hyperscale data centers on his first day in office, and hasn’t ruled out a permanent extension. In one ad, Jolly puts data centers in the same breath as crime in a list of things he doesn’t want in Florida.

His Republican opponent, Congressman Byron Donalds, has previously supported data center development in the state and said Florida is “wide open” to build without destroying the state’s beauty. He’s more recently changed his tune though, and while he still doesn’t want to outright ban data centers, he’s tried to assure voters that he’d support policies protecting them from associated risks like higher energy costs. In July, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would require data center developers to fund the energy and water needed to run their operations. He’s also supported a state law with some similar requirements and environmental guardrails. “In my Florida, if you don’t protect our pocketbooks and our people, you won’t build data centers, period,” he assures voters in one ad. Energy experts have warned, however, that Donalds’ pledge to lean on nuclear and natural gas could actually raise costs for consumers.

Despite these efforts, he’s been branded as “Data Center Donalds” by opponents, and polling suggests he may have to fight for conservative voters who also strongly oppose data center development. An October NBC6/Telemundo Station Group poll found that 45 percent of likely voter respondents opposed data centers in Florida, with 38 percent in support and 17 percent undecided. A higher percentage opposed data centers in their own communities, at 59 percent. Still, the poll found Donalds has a lead of 48 percent to Jolly’s 41 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percent. Ten percent of respondents were still undecided.

Pennsylvania gubernatorial race

In one of the country’s relatively few purple states, both candidates for governor have accused each other of changing their rhetoric on data centers just to get votes. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity each appear to have hardened their stances amid the widespread backlash to data center development, even though they previously touted opportunity in such projects.

Shapiro proudly announced a $20 billion investment from Amazon last year that would bring new data centers to the state, and credited Pennsylvania’s new fast track permitting program in helping lure the investment. But this year, Shapiro has tempered his enthusiasm, signing an executive order in August prohibiting nondisclosure agreements for data center developers and taking AI data center proposals off of the fast track. Shapiro has said his views evolved based on community feedback.

But Garrity, too, has seemed to turn against data centers as the election has drawn closer. In a radio interview last year, she said rural parts of the state would be “perfect places to put data centers,” and they’d be largely welcomed based on the economic opportunity they’d bring. She also praised the Amazon investment Shapiro secured at the time, though it’s now a target of some of her attack ads. This year, she has said data center developers must engage the community rather than “jam it down their throats,” and she supports a pause on development lasting no more than three years, according to Spotlight PA.

An early October Quinnipiac University poll of likely Pennsylvania voters found 64 percent believed AI data centers in the state would do more harm than good, with a plus or minus 3.9 percent margin of error. But a far larger portion of Democratic respondents were wary of them, with 80 percent saying they’d do more harm than good. That suggests it may be even more essential for Shapiro to shore up his position for his base, though the poll had him leading 59 percent to Garrity’s 34 percent.

Ohio Senate race

In the battle for Ohio’s Senate seat, data centers are both “the new ingredient (and the new problem),” according to a leaked National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) memo. Republican incumbent Jon Husted and Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown, who’s fighting to win back his former seat, “are in a dead heat,” the NRSC warned in August. And data centers, the group added, “are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

As the NRSC identified, Brown has made his opposition to data centers a central tenet of his campaign, labeling Husted “the face of data centers” in the state. Brown has hammered Husted over his past support for data centers as lieutenant governor, where he helped install tax breaks. Husted has said he believes local communities should be able to decide whether to bring in data centers, and that some may find the revenue useful.

“If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice”

At least as of August, the NRSC still believed voters favored that approach over sweeping bans but acknowledged that current perception is negative. The group warned that losing the Ohio Senate seat could endanger future support for data centers. “If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one,” the memo says.

Husted introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would require large load customers like data centers to cover their own energy costs and the infrastructure upgrades needed to accommodate them. The bill passed the House and was seen as a potential life raft for Husted, but narrowly failed to pass the Senate, even with a handful of Democrats voting in favor. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up, and a RealClear Polling average of recent surveys shows Brown with a slight edge.

Michigan Senate race

Data centers are a hot topic across two key races in Michigan with razor-thin margins. The state is handling dozens of new data center proposals, and both candidates for Michigan’s open Senate seat support a moratorium. Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers supports a one-year pause but opposes a federal ban, while Democratic candidate and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed says there should be “no more data centers until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers’ moratorium support came days after The Lever reported on his investments that reportedly stand to gain from the buildout.

El-Sayed put his stake in the ground on data centers relatively early, compared to other Democrats across the country. In February, Politico wrote that “underdogs” like El-Sayed were centering data centers in their primary campaigns, raising what’s now a common topic in campaign ads. El-Sayed is also now locked in what the Cook Political Report rates as a dead heat with Rogers, in a race that could determine the balance of power in Congress. Rogers and El-Sayed are competing for a seat currently held by Democrat Gary Peters, who isn’t seeking another term.

In another toss-up race, Democratic organizer William Lawrence is challenging Republican incumbent Tom Barrett for his House seat. Lawrence called for a year-long federal moratorium on new data center construction during his primary campaign, and when he won the nomination, his supporters reportedly chanted, “data centers lost.” In the general election, data centers have continued to be a central theme. Barrett introduced two bills this summer that would strengthen local decision-making on data center development and bar federal lawmakers from signing non-disclosure agreements about data centers. Lawrence’s data center plan includes environmental standards, worker protections, and “zoning buffers” for data center development.

Wisconsin gubernatorial race

Wisconsin is another state where both gubernatorial candidates have backed away from previous support for data centers, but neither has gone as far as to call for a moratorium. Democratic nominee and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, for example, set himself apart from his progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong by declining to oppose a development moratorium that she supported.

Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee, similarly opposes a moratorium in favor of data center guardrails, and voted for a bill allowing faster permitting for data center projects. But Tiffany has still tried to label his opponent as “data center David Crowley,” pointing to past comments he made saying the state shouldn’t “automatically roll back all data center tax incentives.” More recently, Crowley has said he would sign a bill repealing tax subsidies for the facilities. Cook Political Report says the race is a dead heat.

Nevada gubernatorial race

Nevada’s Democratic Party created an entire website branding Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo “data center Joe,” highlighting his past supportive comments about data centers and money his campaign took from AI-connected donors. Lombardo, locked in a tight race to keep his seat, has fought the accusations. He introduced an executive order last month that ties tax incentives to developers covering power costs and meeting water use standards, empowering the state to claw back money from those who violate it. But Democratic challenger and attorney general Aaron Ford has said he’d go further, pausing tax breaks entirely for new data centers.

At the same time, Ford has been criticized for championing a 2015 bill enshrining data center tax breaks. Ford said his thinking has evolved with new information, and that “the data centers of 11 years ago are not the data centers of 2026.” The issue is particularly salient in a state that’s experiencing significant water issues. The Cook Political Report says the race is a toss-up.

Georgia gubernatorial race

Swing state Georgia has been called “one of the nation’s most attractive markets for AI, hyperscale cloud and enterprise data center development,” and its gubernatorial candidates — Democratic nominee and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican nominee and healthcare executive Rick Jackson — have sparred over each other’s data center records. Bottoms supports a pause on development to evaluate environmental and cost effects, while Jackson says it should be up to local communities to decide whether to bring a data center in.

At a recent debate in the toss-up race, Bottoms said her opponent “cannot be trusted” on the topic based on his investment in a Texas data center. Jackson shot back that Bottoms approved and gave tax breaks to multiple data centers as mayor, which Bottoms denied, saying she only approved one non-hyperscale data center that wasn’t near a residential community. While Bottoms led the Invest Atlanta board in 2018, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported, the group approved up to $440 million in bonds for a mixed-use project at Georgia Tech that included a data center. This was not a “direct financing mechanism” but did help the project get tax abatement, the AJC wrote, and its data center was far smaller than those mainly at issue today.

Arizona gubernatorial and AG races

In dry Arizona where concerns about water are a top issue for many voters, the most interesting conflict is within parties, not across them. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs and Attorney General Kris Mayes are both locked in close races with their respective Republican challengers, Rep. Andy Biggs and state legislator Warren Petersen. But the two Democrats are split over how to regulate data centers: Mayes supports a statewide pause on development, while Hobbs opposes one.

In dry Arizona, the most interesting conflict is within parties, not across them

Mayes says the state should “take a beat” to evaluate water and energy needs, a move Petersen has criticized in a rare outright defense of data centers, saying, “If you like your tech and your phone and your computer and the stuff you can use that for, you probably think data centers are important.” Hobbs, meanwhile, says data centers are here to stay, and the state should instead figure out how to best make them work for communities. That puts her significantly closer to her Republican opponent, who similarly opposes a moratorium.

Iowa gubernatorial race

Iowa’s open governor’s seat is another close race where data centers are taking center stage. The state economic development authority says Iowa’s wind energy and low construction and business costs have attracted developers there, but their growth has also brought concerns to local communities.

Democratic nominee and state auditor Rob Sand has not supported a blanket moratorium but says he would end tax breaks for data centers, make them cover their own costs, and keep NDAs from shielding deals from communities. Republican nominee and businessman Zach Lahn called for a moratorium on new development and eliminating tax incentives for them.

OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.

OpenAI has announced that its AI models have made several scientific discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics.

The AI giant said on Monday that the three new discoveries concerned the fields of harmonic analysis, complexity theory and quantum field theory.

Among the discoveries, AI models proved the local smoothing conjecture, one of the central propositions of harmonic analysis, in every spatial dimension for the first time, according to OpenAI.

Researchers in harmonic analysis, a branch of mathematics that studies how complex signals and functions can be broken down into elementary waves, had previously only proved the theory in three dimensions.

‘Historic development’

Alex Iosevich, a professor of mathematics at the University of Rochester who specialises in harmonic analysis, said OpenAI appeared to have “cracked” the conjecture in a “historic development”.

“The conjecture was formulated by my PhD adviser, Chris Sogge, so it is near and dear to my heart, and the news was a shock at first,” Iosevich told Al Jazeera.

“Now I am filled with joy and optimism, because the scientific enterprise as a whole is going to make giant leaps as a result of the AI revolution, and we have the chance to be a part of this historic development.”

Iosevich said he expected the field of theoretical mathematics to “change drastically” due to AI.

“I feel a twinge of sadness as a result,” Iosevich said.

“Many theoretical mathematicians I know feel the same way, but I firmly believe that these feelings will soon give way to the realisation that there is so much we can now accomplish.”

“Problems in pure mathematics did not arise in a vacuum,” he added. “Many of them came out of concrete physical considerations, and these connections can now be explored rapidly and decisively.”

According to OpenAI’s announcement, its models also disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which relates to the time it takes to solve complex computational problems, and provided “mathematically rigorous [proof of the] existence” of quantum chromodynamics, which studies the interaction of quarks and gluons.

The ChatGPT creator said it had reached out to scientists outside the company to turn its “raw research data into scientific understanding”.

The San Francisco-based company said it decided on several different methods for releasing the findings based on consultations with three expert groups chosen to act as “shepherds”.

While the groups collaborating on the mathematics and computer science problems opted to make the AI-produced data public immediately, the physics group decided to defer the release in order to write up their own interpretation of the findings, OpenAI said.

“All of these approaches involve tradeoffs,” OpenAI said.

“On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community,” the $852bn start-up said.

“On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.”

OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.

Last month, Claude creator Anthropic announced the discovery of a new enzyme said to resemble CRISPR, the groundbreaking gene editing mechanism used in treating conditions such as cancer and sickle cell disease.

Anthropic’s announcement drew mixed reactions among scientists.

While some researchers hailed the finding as an exciting development, others suggested that the AI company had exaggerated its significance.

articles.title: How OpenAI turned its coding tools into dots, an always-on personal assistant
articles.summary: Alexander Embiricos, the OpenAI executive responsible for dots, never wants to have a meeting with someone else's AI agent.
articles.preview: The always-on AI personal assistant, which keeps working in the background even when you aren’t asking it to, is this year’s answer to the question of how people will actually use deep learning models. The startup Instinct became an overnight sensation, and Meta put the full force of its marketing behind its assistant, Muse. OpenAI wasn’t going to be left out. The company released dots, its assistant offering, at its developer day in late September.
articles.body:
The always-on AI personal assistant, which keeps working in the background even when you aren’t asking it to, is this year’s answer to the question of how people will actually use deep learning models. The startup Instinct became an overnight sensation, and Meta put the full force of its marketing behind its assistant, Muse.

OpenAI wasn’t going to be left out. The company released dots, its assistant offering, at its developer day in late September. Alexander Embiricos, who leads OpenAI’s enterprise product team, joined us at TechCrunch Disrupt this month to explain where the product came from—starting with the question of why so many companies seem to be turning to cutesy mascots as avatars for their trillion-parameter matrix multiplication machines.

“There’s kind of this convergent evolution happening,” Embiricos said of the efforts to build AI assistants. “As we were working on the product, we realized if we could frame this as, it’s an entity and it’s a single conversation, not many different conversations….it starts to become intuitive.”

The assistant is available in the ChatGPT desktop and mobile apps to subscribers on the Pro tier or higher, with plans starting at $100 a month. Once it is connected to your calendar, email, computer and other tools, the agent tries to help you get your work done.

Embiricos points out that you could achieve much of dots’ functionality with Open AI’s Codex app, its coding tool, released at the beginning of this year. But that requires more work and hand-holding. He recalled celebrating when his wife started leaving her computer on all night so that her agents could keep working.

“On the product team, what I think about is, how do we make this intuitive and useful to people?” he told Disrupt attendees. “A lot of that isn’t building some new piece of tech into the product; it’s how you frame it to the user and how it feels.”

The path from chat bot to coding tool to personal assistant

Making the technology feel intuitive meant repackaging the functionality of the company’s models into something more accessible, a path it was already on as it spun ChatGPT Work out of the agentic coding tools it had built for software engineers. Even the name—a play on the negative space inside of OpenAI’s logo—is intended “to feel like just something that could eventually be ubiquitous.” (Asked when he learned that rival AI entrepreneur Elon Musk owns the dot.com URL, Embiricos said, “I found out very late.”)

The idea of a persistent agent is that it doesn’t need prompting. For OpenAI, means more token usage, and for users, a more pro-active assistant “that’s sort of thinking about you and thinking how to help you,” as Embiricos put it.

In our testing, the assistant’s ability to think ahead is apparent and often useful, but it isn’t quite there yet. It will flag calendar conflicts and upcoming deadlines, but not necessarily in the most timely fashion.

“The first time it told me about one of those [conflicts]—this is like early in development—it told me three minutes before the thing,” Embiricos says of his dot. “It’s like, ‘Hey, this thing is coming up. You might want to do something about it.’ I only have three minutes!”

Embiricos expects the timing to improve over time, but the proactive approach is key to the product. “I was hearing about an engineer at a drone delivery startup, and they were saying, ‘We had this outage, and by the time I noticed that the outage was going on, my dot had already noticed the outage was happening, had already analyzed the outage, and had come to me with useful information for how we could resolve the outage.’”

Giving dot the keys

As with most AI agent use cases, there’s a tension between the personal information an AI model needs to be useful and exactly how much personal data you are exposing to a software company. Muse has been criticized for the profiles it builds of your family and friends, which the software uses to know, say, what kind of restaurant you might want to go to with a specific pal, but could also add incredible value to Meta’s advertising business. Does dots collect similar data?

“Yes, we have a thing that we built into dots, which we call proactive research,” Embiricos said. “On a cadence, it will think about what it knows about you, what is the conversation that it’s had, and then what have you given it access to that it can think about, and then it will go and research, ‘What could I do to be more helpful to you?’ And then, basically, it will propose that.”

It’s difficult to separate the data needs of the agent from that of its parent corporation. Hark, a start-up developing its own AI personal assistant, is explicit in pointing out it that it doesn’t collect data to fuel an advertising business the way that OpenAI and Meta do.

With dots, OpenAI says that the agent has the same privacy controls as ChatGPT itself: Users can turn off model training (stopping OpenAI from using their conversations to improve its AI), and control what resources it accesses within your computer and how. Still, those controls aren’t granular and the app can be pushy. For example, it refuses to accept read-only access to cloud drives.

“What I think we need to do is basically build out super, super, super granular controls,” Embiricos said, but he pointed to the model’s intelligence and discretion as the other side of this coin.

“This is actually something we kind of got some flack about when we launched,” Embiricos said. “We had really conservative defaults over what the agent would do, and it would ask for permission a lot. I remember knowing that we were going to see that feedback, but thinking, ‘This is okay, we can tune that over time.’”

Can personal AI agents scale?

The other big question about AI agents is whether they can scale. They’re fun when only a few people have them, and stories of agents snagging hard-to-get reservations abound. But businesses don’t necessarily like dealing with agents and might not be equipped to. People certainly don’t like dealing with them (note: stop having your AI agents pitch me), and Embiricos is among those people. He also has a human assistant because OpenAI’s corporate partners want to interact with a person, he said, adding, “I personally never intend to have a meeting with someone else’s agent.”

If the AI industry is right that agents are our future, can we get there without overwhelming the infrastructure that our world currently runs on, from businesses and websites to payment networks?

“At OpenAI…we’re not always moving the fastest in terms of shipping the next ability for the agent to work with the world,” he said. “When we do, we’re doing it really closely in collaboration with the rest of the ecosystem. I probably can’t say too much here, but we’re deep in lots of conversations with payment processors.”

Letting an AI assistant spend money through partnerships with payment companies would be a potentially lucrative first for OpenAI, but also a big ask for consumers. Giving an assistant access to my email inbox already feels like a big ask, but my bank account is off limits. For now.

articles.body:
Less than a month after its mass release of hundreds of manuscripts that it said contained solutions to long-standing mathematics questions, OpenAI is back with three more “major” discoveries in math, computer science, and physics. What’s different this time is the choice to have external experts that OpenAI describes as “shepherds” guiding the results in computer science and physics, while for the math problem it says that they advised it to release the AI output for researchers to work through their own explanations.

This time OpenAI says it’s taking new advice from scientists on how to release the results.

OpenAI results added to GitHub today:

Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation. The proof uses an auxiliary partial differential equation to establish Sogge’s local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension at least two. It also yields the Kakeya maximal and dimension conjectures and Stein’s spherical restriction estimates throughout the interior of the conjectured range. We are releasing the model output directly, as we did in our October 6 release.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. The paper gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas in subexponential time and polynomial space. The case of 3-SAT refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis. An independent working group of computer scientists led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi, and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof. At the group’s request, we are making the materials public immediately so others can examine them as well.

This approach could have its own issues, the company admits, and the AGMAI panel of math advisers OpenAI put together just said yesterday that “we recommend that AI companies do not adopt” the practices of designating certain people to receive the output first, citing unequal access, borrowed reputation, and biased selection as a few of the issues. Instead, they recommended that in the future, AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with Lean-formalized proofs, info on how the problems were chosen, funding for people working on understanding the results, and other information.

The physics information has not been released in full, but is a “mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics.” According to OpenAI, “David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work.”

The computer science collaboration is said to prove that the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which has been widely believed to be true, is actually false. OpenAI says verification of the result will be guided by a group of three experts that includes UC San Diego’s Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who were part of the group that originally proposed it in 1999, as well as MIT professor Ryan Williams. The group decided to release the AI output write-up and Lean proof on GitHub today.

They also released an open letter to the community asking for input on how to examine the claim, and about setting norms for dealing with AI-generated breakthroughs:

We would welcome discussion of three broader questions:

What expectations should govern early access to AI-generated results, disclosure of conflicts of interest, and the use of unpublished material for subsequent research?

How should credit recognize both new discoveries and the work of checking, fixing, simplifying, explaining, and extending them?

How can we support students and researchers as methods and research directions change, while preserving the understanding and judgment needed to question results and develop new ideas?

There’s similar documentation for the math breakthrough, where its model “produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions.” Just a few months ago, NYU professor Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal by the International Mathematical Union for resolving the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions.
